etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French monotonie, from Late Latin monotonia, from Ancient Greek μονοτονία (monotonía, “sameness of tone, monotony”).

definitions.definition: Tedium as a result of repetition or a lack of variety.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter II, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume I, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 24:
quote.text: It matters little to trace the rapidity of the land journey, or the monotony of the sea voyage—alike unmarked by adventure. Robert Evelyn landed at Southampton,...

quote.citation: 1907, Arthur Conan Doyle, chapter 1, in Through the Magic Door‎[1], archived from the original on 12 April 2011:
quote.text: Yet second-hand romance and second-hand emotion are surely better than the dull, soul-killing monotony which life brings to most of the human race.
Transform my death into a conduitThis body separate from the fear of fearInside a coping mechanism of monotonyI will destroy the double vision that I was forced to leave

definitions.definition: (mathematics) The property of a monotonic function.
The quality of having an unvarying tone or pitch.
